title: 7 Poinsettia Mistakes That KILL It Before Christmas (Keep It Red)

scenes.text: Sweetheart, every December, Americans buy more than thirty million poinsettias. And most of them are dropping their leaves and dead by New Year's Day. People think they just don't have a green thumb. That's not it. Almost every poinsettia dies from the same seven mistakes, and most of them happen before you even get it home. My mother kept one poinsettia alive for eleven years.
scenes.query: wilted poinsettia dropping leaves
scenes.caption: DEAD BY NEW YEAR'S

scenes.text: So tonight I'm giving you the seven mistakes that kill a poinsettia before Christmas, and how to keep yours red and full until spring. And stay with me, because at the end I'll tell you my mother's secret for making it turn red again the next Christmas, with nothing but a closet and a calendar.
scenes.query: bright red poinsettia by window
scenes.caption: A CLOSET AND A CALENDAR

scenes.text: The poinsettia comes from Mexico, honey, where it grows wild into a bush ten feet tall. In Mexico, they call it the flower of the Holy Night. There's an old story about a poor little girl who had no gift to bring to the Christmas Eve service, so she picked some weeds by the road. And when she laid them at the altar, they burst into red stars. In a minute I'll tell you how it got its American name.
scenes.query: wild poinsettia bush in Mexico
scenes.caption: FLOWER OF THE HOLY NIGHT

scenes.text: It's named after Joel Poinsett, the first American minister to Mexico, back in the eighteen twenties. He was a plant lover, and he sent cuttings home to his greenhouse in South Carolina. Then a family of growers in California turned it into the Christmas plant, and by the nineteen fifties, there was a poinsettia on every church altar and in every bank lobby in America. And here's something most people don't know, sweetheart. The red parts aren't flowers at all.
scenes.query: church altar filled with poinsettias 1950s
scenes.caption: NOT FLOWERS AT ALL

scenes.text: The red parts are leaves, honey. Special leaves called bracts. The real flowers are those tiny little yellow-green buttons in the very center. And that matters, because those little buttons tell you how fresh the plant is. That's the first thing I'm going to teach you. My mother taught me in the grocery store when I was nine, and I've never bought a bad poinsettia since.
scenes.query: close up of poinsettia center yellow buds
scenes.caption: THE LITTLE BUTTONS

scenes.text: My mother's first one came from the bank, honey. In nineteen fifty-three, the First National Bank on Main Street gave a little poinsettia to every customer who opened a Christmas club account. My mother saved fifty cents a week, and she got her poinsettia. She was so proud of it. She set it on the radiator, the warmest spot in the house, so it would be cozy. It was dead in six days. I'll tell you what she learned from that in a minute.
scenes.query: small poinsettia on 1950s radiator
scenes.caption: DEAD IN SIX DAYS

scenes.text: Mistake number one is buying an old plant. Look at those tiny buttons in the center. If they're tight and green or yellow, with no pollen, the plant is young, and it'll stay beautiful for months. If they're open and dusty with yellow pollen, or if they've fallen off, that plant is already old, and it'll drop its leaves in a couple of weeks. Also check the soil. If it's bone dry or soaking wet, walk away.
scenes.query: checking poinsettia center in store
scenes.caption: CHECK THE CENTER

scenes.text: Mistake number two is the trip home. Poinsettias are tropical, honey. They can't stand the cold. Even five minutes at below fifty degrees, walking across a parking lot in the wind, can damage the leaves. And you won't see it for a few days. Then they all drop at once, and you think you did something wrong at home. Always have the store wrap it in a paper sleeve or a bag, and put it in the warm car, not the trunk.
scenes.query: poinsettia wrapped in paper sleeve in car
scenes.caption: NEVER IN THE COLD

scenes.text: If Grandma's tips are helping you, tap the like button for me, sweetheart. It helps more people find these videos. Mistake number three is the foil wrapper. Those pretty foil sleeves around the pot hold water like a bathtub. When you water the plant, the water runs out the bottom and sits in the foil, and the roots rot. You'll see the leaves turn yellow and droop. Poke a few holes in the bottom of the foil, or take the pot out to water it.
scenes.query: poinsettia pot in shiny foil wrapper
scenes.caption: THE FOIL IS A BATHTUB

scenes.text: Mistake number four is watering on a schedule. People water every Sunday, whether the plant needs it or not. Poke your finger in the soil every day or two. When the top inch feels dry, water it well, at the sink, until it runs out the bottom. Let it drain completely. Then put it back. Too much water kills more poinsettias than too little. In a minute I'll tell you the worst place in the house to put it.
scenes.query: finger testing soil in poinsettia pot
scenes.caption: THE FINGER TEST

scenes.text: And don't feed it while it's in bloom, sweetheart. People think plant food will help a drooping poinsettia, but it's not hungry, it's in bloom. Feeding it now can burn the roots. Save the plant food for spring, when it starts putting out new green leaves. Right now, all it needs is water when it's dry, light, and warmth. Simple. Just like a houseguest at Christmas.
scenes.query: plant food bottle on shelf unused
scenes.caption: NOT HUNGRY

scenes.text: Mistake number five is the wrong spot. The worst places are right by the front door, where cold air blows in every time somebody comes and goes, and right next to a heater vent or a radiator, where the hot, dry air cooks it. Put it near a sunny window, but not touching the cold glass. Poinsettias like the same temperature you do, between sixty and seventy degrees. If you're comfortable, it's comfortable.
scenes.query: poinsettia away from heater vent near window
scenes.caption: IF YOU'RE COMFORTABLE

scenes.text: Mistake number six is not enough light. People put their poinsettia on the coffee table in the middle of the room, or on the dining table, far from any window, because it looks pretty there. And it does, for about a week. Then it starts dropping leaves. Keep it by a bright window during the day, at least six hours of light. Move it to the table for company in the evening, and back to the window in the morning.
scenes.query: poinsettia on dining table for dinner guests
scenes.caption: MOVE IT FOR COMPANY

scenes.text: So far, check the center, keep it warm on the way home, poke the foil, the finger test, away from drafts, and plenty of light. Mistake number seven is believing they're deadly poisonous. For seventy years, people threw them out because they heard poinsettias would kill their cat or their grandbaby. That's an old wives' tale, honey. Studies have shown they're only mildly irritating. A curious pet might get a tummy ache, or a child might get a rash from the milky sap.
scenes.query: cat sniffing poinsettia plant
scenes.caption: NOT DEADLY

scenes.text: Still keep it out of reach of puppies and little ones, sweetheart, because nobody wants an upset tummy at Christmas. And wash your hands if you get the white sap on them. Some people with latex allergies are sensitive to it. But you don't need to throw it away or live without one. My mother had a poinsettia, a cat named Biscuit, and two children, and all of us survived just fine.
scenes.query: poinsettia on high shelf with cat below
scenes.caption: WE ALL SURVIVED

scenes.text: A few more tips, honey. If you have a big poinsettia and it's looking leggy, group it with two or three smaller ones in a basket. They hold each other up and look like one big, expensive arrangement. The white and pink ones are just as easy to keep as the red. And if you want it to last, buy it early in December, not on Christmas Eve, when the stores are selling the ones that sat by the drafty door for three weeks.
scenes.query: basket of red and white poinsettias grouped
scenes.caption: GROUP THEM

scenes.text: After Christmas, keep watering it and keep it in the sunny window, and it'll stay pretty well into March. In spring, when the leaves start to fade, cut the stems back to about six inches tall. In May, put it outside in a shady spot for the summer, and feed it once a month with plant food. By September, it'll be a big, bushy green plant. Bring it inside before the first frost. Stay with me, because now comes the secret.
scenes.query: green poinsettia plant outdoors in summer
scenes.caption: CUT IT BACK IN SPRING

scenes.text: Here's my mother's secret, sweetheart. Poinsettias only turn red when the nights get long. In the wild, that happens on its own. But in a house, with the lamps on every evening, it never turns red again. So starting on the first of October, every single evening at five o'clock, my mother put her poinsettia in the hall closet. And every morning at eight, she took it back out to the window. Fourteen hours of total darkness every night.
scenes.query: woman putting poinsettia in closet in evening
scenes.caption: FOURTEEN HOURS OF DARK

scenes.text: She did it for eight to ten weeks, honey, with a little calendar taped inside the closet door, checking off the days. Even one night with the light on could spoil it. My father teased her and called it her baby that went to bed at five. And every year, around Thanksgiving, those top leaves started to blush pink, then red. By Christmas, it was as red as the day she bought it. Eleven Christmases, the same plant.
scenes.query: calendar on closet door with checked days
scenes.caption: SHE CHECKED OFF THE DAYS

scenes.text: Buy a good one this year, sweetheart, and keep it warm and bright. Tell me in the comments, does your poinsettia make it to New Year's? Be honest. There are more of my Christmas tips in the playlist right there on your screen. Good night, honey. Merry Christmas.
scenes.query: healthy red poinsettia by Christmas tree
scenes.caption: BUY A GOOD ONE
